title: Average
shortDescription: Switch between total and average instead of adding values one by one — and know when 'average speed' secretly means harmonic mean.
genZNote: Average is just Total wearing a disguise. Rip the disguise off — multiply back to Total — and half these questions solve themselves.

sections.heading: Core Idea
sections.body: Average = (Sum of values) / (Number of values). The single most useful habit for exam Average questions is to flip this around: Total = Average × Number of items — most 'average' word problems are actually Total problems wearing a disguise.

sections.heading: Total ↔ Average — the Core Technique
sections.body: Whenever a question mixes averages of different-sized groups (e.g. 'average of 10 numbers is 20, average of a different 5 numbers is 30, find the combined average'), convert every average to a total first, combine the totals, then divide by the combined count. Do not attempt to average the averages directly unless every group is the same size.

steps.name: Worked example
steps.explanation: 10 numbers average 20 (total = 200). 5 numbers average 30 (total = 150). Combined average = (200+150)/(10+5) = 350/15.
steps.purpose: Convert to totals, combine, then divide — never average two averages of unequal-sized groups directly.

sections.heading: Replacement / Change-in-Average Shortcut
sections.body: When one value in a group is replaced by another, the average shifts by exactly (change in that one value) ÷ (number of items) — you don't need to recompute the whole total from scratch.
bullets: Example: the average weight of 20 students is 55 kg. One student weighing 40 kg leaves and a new student joins, raising the average by 0.5 kg. New student's weight = 40 + (0.5 × 20) = 50 kg.

sections.heading: Average Speed for Equal Distances — Not a Simple Mean
sections.body: For a journey covered at two different speeds over EQUAL distances (not equal times), the correct average speed is the harmonic-mean-based formula (2×S1×S2)/(S1+S2) — NOT the simple arithmetic mean (S1+S2)/2 — because more TIME is spent at the slower speed, pulling the true average down.

steps.name: Worked example
steps.explanation: A car travels A to B at 40 km/h and returns the same distance at 60 km/h. Simple (wrong) mean: (40+60)/2 = 50 km/h.
steps.purpose: Shows why the naive approach is tempting but wrong.

steps.name: Correct method
steps.purpose: The correct, exam-expected answer — always lower than the simple mean for unequal speeds over equal distances.

sections.heading: Common Traps
bullets: Taking the simple arithmetic mean of two speeds for an equal-distance journey — use the harmonic-mean formula instead.
Averaging two group averages directly when the groups have different sizes — convert to totals first.
Forgetting that a single outlier can shift an average a lot; unlike the median, the average is sensitive to extreme values.

sections.heading: Exam Strategy
bullets: Whenever you see 'average', silently rewrite it as Total = Average × Count in your head before doing anything else.
Spot 'equal distance, different speeds' phrasing immediately — it's the exam's favourite average-speed trap.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Average = Total ÷ Count; most exam Average questions are solved fastest by converting to Total first.
keyFacts: Change in average from a replacement = (change in value) ÷ (number of items).
Average speed for equal distances at different speeds = (2×S1×S2)/(S1+S2), not the simple mean.
commonConfusion: Equal-DISTANCE journeys need the harmonic-mean average-speed formula; equal-TIME journeys at different speeds DO average with a simple mean.

highYieldFacts: Convert every average to a total before combining groups of different sizes.
commonTraps: Using the simple mean for an equal-distance, different-speed journey.
Averaging averages of unequal-sized groups directly instead of via totals.
mustRemember: Total = Average × Count — the single most reused rewrite in this topic.
